title: Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching for Quantum Error Codes
claim: A raw error pattern is converted into a weighted graph, and a learned module predicts the weights that a classical solver uses for the final output.
layout: 3 panels: two top, one bottom; left-to-right flow, dashed module box
description: The figure has three panels. Panel (a), top left, shows a square lattice with qubits drawn as circles. Three orange circles marked X are bit-flip errors. Four pink shaded plaquettes numbered 3, 6, 8 and 9 mark the syndrome defects. Grey dashed circles lie along the boundary. Panel (b), top right, shows those four defects as nodes of a complete graph. The edges carry integer weights. Panel (c), along the bottom, is a left-to-right block diagram. A graph G=(V,E) is split into a node branch (preprocessing plus a GNN) and an edge branch (edge preprocessing). Both branches are combined by a circled plus into a Transformer Encoder, all inside a dashed box labeled QWP. The encoder outputs a re-weighted graph (w_pred), which goes into an MWPM block that produces M. The purple boxes draw the eye first.
caption: Overview of the proposed decoding pipeline. (a) Three physical errors on the lattice generate four syndrome defects. (b) These defects form the vertices of a complete graph used for matching. (c) The complete NMWPM architecture processes this graph to predict dynamic edge weights for the final correction.
abstract: Realizing the full potential of quantum computation requires Quantum Error Correction (QEC). QEC reduces error rates by encoding logical information across redundant physical qubits, enabling errors to be detected and corrected. A common decoder used for this task is Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) a graph-based algorithm that relies on edge weights to identify the most likely error chains. In this work, we propose a data-driven decoder named Neural Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (NMWPM). Our decoder utilizes a hybrid architecture that integrates Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to extract local syndrome features and Transformers to capture long-range global dependencies, which are then used to predict dynamic edge weights for the MWPM decoder. To facilitate training through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm, we formulate a novel proxy loss function that enables end-to-end optimization. Our findings on the toric code under depolarizing noise demonstrate thresholds of 17.9% and 10.95%, nearing the 18.9% and 11.0% maximum likelihood bounds, highlighting the advantage of hybrid decoders that combine the predictive capabilities of neural networks with the algorithmic structure of classical matching.
